text: Because Saturn is a gas giant, the final orbit can be lowered until the spacecraft enters the upper atmosphere and is destroyed. If NASA just left Cassini deorbiting freely, its path could cross the orbits of moons, especially Enceladus or Titan, where a subsurface ocean or thick atmosphere makes contamination a real concern. The instruments, residual fluids, and possibly surviving microbes would not be good news for a world that might support life. So the deorbit burn was timed and aimed so Cassini would intersect Saturn's atmosphere, not a moon. The crash is a deliberate disposal method, and it ends the mission.

The part that hurts is doing more than it looks like from the outside. Your standing leg isn't truly stationary. Even when the board is gliding, your muscles are making constant small adjustments to keep the balance from tipping, and that continuous low-level effort adds up quickly. The shock from the road also goes through that leg, so the joints and tendons are absorbing impacts while the leg is planted. That is a different kind of load from the pushing leg, which gets a brief rest between pushes. The stationary leg does not.

It is a bit unfair how it feels. You keep seeing advice about ankle strength, and some of that makes sense. But for a leg that is mostly standing, the problem is less about a single weak muscle and more about the whole chain: foot, ankle, knee, hip. When you stand on a moving board, your body has to be constantly micro-correcting. That is tiring work, and the soreness is the result of accumulated strain, not an injury in the usual sense.

The reason this shows up as pain rather than just tiredness is that the muscles are being used isometrically, holding position instead of moving through a range. Holding is harder on the tissues than repetitive motion. Add the uneven ground and the way the board shifts under you, and the leg is under load the entire ride.

A few things can make it better. Keeping your knees slightly bent gives the joints a bit of give, and you will not be locking the leg rigid. If the pain is sharp rather than a dull ache, that changes things. Dull aches after skating are usually just muscle fatigue; sharp or lingering pain can point to a tendon or joint problem, and you would want to watch it.

So the answer is that your stationary leg is not resting at all. It is balancing, absorbing impact, and holding position, and that sustained low-level work is what makes it hurt.

It’s a bit of a category mistake. “Afro-American” (and the more common “African-American”) doesn’t mean the person was born in Africa or that most black Americans are currently African. It points to ancestry: the majority of Black Americans are descendants of Africans who were enslaved and brought to the US, so the label reflects where that lineage began, not where the individual lives. Some Black Americans are immigrants from Africa, some from the Caribbean, some are mixed-race, and some don’t identify with the term at all, but for the demographic group the connection is ancestral. That’s why the name can feel odd when someone is American-born and has no family in Africa: the label is shorthand for a historical origin, not a passport check. You can be fully American while still carrying that African heritage in your genealogy. It’s an ethnic/cultural identifier, not a statement about current residency. It’s also worth noting that “Afro-American” isn’t an official census category; the term is mostly used by media and academics. Some people prefer “Black American” or just “Black.” The label is a cultural shorthand for the African diaspora in the US, not evidence that every Black person has a family member living in Africa.

Mostly through local supply chains rather than fresh imports: captured enemy stores, stockpiles, black markets, and small local workshops, with some regional smuggling (Lebanon and the Gulf) and state or factional supply from allies such as Russia and Iran-backed groups. It happens often. They still get them because in a fragmented war, armed power is the only leverage that really matters. Factions keep arming because they do not trust anyone, want protection, and need to hold positions or project strength. The weapons keep flowing because each side wants a stronger hand for the next negotiation or next attack, almost always.

I think the premise is a bit too neat. Drugs are not all bad; some are useful. But the drugs you mention, heroin and cocaine, are the ones people use for the high, and that high is exactly the problem. The pleasure comes from pushing the reward circuitry hard, and the same chemistry that makes it feel good is what gets out of balance when the system is overloaded. That's not a separate flaw; it's the mechanism. If a drug gave intense euphoria without any downside, it would have to hit the reward centre while leaving the rest of the body untouched, which is a tall order for a substance that acts on such central systems.

Many adverse effects are not separate side effects in the usual sense. They are what happens when the nervous system is driven beyond its normal range. Breathing, heart rate, temperature, appetite, sleep, hormones, all respond when you stimulate the brain that hard. Tolerance is another part of the story. The brain compensates for strong stimulation by adjusting its own chemistry, so the same dose stops producing the same high. Then the user chases it, and the gap between the old high and the current state becomes withdrawal. That is how many people get into trouble.

There may be drugs with fewer problems, and some drugs are genuinely useful at the right dose. But intense euphoria is a special request. A drug with zero adverse effects would need to be perfectly selective and not disturb the systems the reward circuitry is wired into. In practice, intensity and selectivity don't travel well together. Turning up the pleasurable signal also makes you more likely to affect neighbouring systems. That doesn't mean every euphoric drug is ruinous. It means the claim of zero adverse effects is much harder to make for strong highs than for mild or therapeutic drugs.

The word bad hides a distinction. Some drugs are useful at the right dose, while others become a problem when misused. The ones people take for euphoria are usually the ones where the high is the point, and that is where tolerance, withdrawal and dose-related effects become important. You can imagine a mild euphoric drug with few adverse effects, but the moment you ask for intense pleasure, the body has to pay something. That is not a moral judgment about users; it is just how central nervous system chemistry works.

Hi,
I know the feeling, and yes, it is real. The pain is not a normal headache; it comes from the actual work of a long shopping day. You are walking, standing, and carrying bags, often in shoes that suit her schedule more than your feet. That puts load on your lower back or legs, and the ache builds as the day goes on. It is a bit unfair that you are doing all the carrying while she chooses. Try light bags, comfortable shoes, and short rests if you can. If it keeps coming back, a physio would be wiser than assuming it is just stress.
Thanks

Hi,

Your brother was running a quick cognitive test on you. The repetition of "silk" is mostly a distractor, occupying your working memory so you are less careful with the next question. The real trick is the cows question.

You answered "milk" because of priming and semantic association. When the brain hears "cows", the strongest immediate link in the mental dictionary is "milk" (what they produce), not "water" (what they ingest). Even though you consciously know cows drink water, the prompt triggered the more common, culturally entrenched association. Your factual knowledge got overridden by the brain's automatic associative network.

It is a standard psychological effect. A specific cue activates highly related concepts much faster than deliberate factual recall. You weren't confused about the underlying fact; you just followed the brain's default semantic path. No need to feel silly about it. It is a known cognitive bias, and your brother almost certainly knew you would fall for the trap. Next time he tries this, just answer water and see if he has an explanation ready for you.

Thanks

Hi,

I can help, but I need the specifics from you. Are you asking about budget, mortgages, surveys, or the actual buying process? A few things matter regardless of which part you mean. First, get your finances in order before you commit. You need to know your real affordable limit, not the number a lender quotes off the top of their head. Then get a mortgage in principle, and remember that is not an offer, just permission to start looking. Do not skip a survey because the house looks fine. A basic check will flag structural issues, and a building survey is better if the property is older or has a history. The legal work is also important; you do not sign anything until the solicitor has reviewed the title and any leases or covenants. If you are in a chain, assume delays. Get the timeline written down early. Once you make an offer, keep everything in writing. In the UK, the exchange of contracts is when it becomes binding, and that is the point where your money is at stake, so do not let the solicitor rush you. Send me your actual questions and I will give you straight answers.

Thanks

The difference is mostly in what the formula is balanced for. A 3-in-1 has to clean skin and hair without stripping them, so it tends to use milder surfactants and added conditioning agents, rather than a dedicated shampoo that is engineered for lather, oil removal and scalp health. You can see the split in ingredients: dedicated shampoos often rely on stronger cleansing agents, while 3-in-1s include skin-softening additives and hair-conditioning film-formers. The 2-in-1 already splits the task between hair washing and conditioning, and the 3-in-1 adds a skin-cleansing role. That means the product is a compromise: good for a quick shower or short hair, but if you have long or thick hair, you will probably still want separate shampoo, conditioner and bodywash. Individual products can be stronger and more targeted; a 3-in-1 is convenience, not a full replacement. For everyday use it can be fine, but for hair that needs real conditioning, the extra rinse and separate products still matter. In practice, the 3-in-1 is often marketed for travel or quick routines; if you want a full wash and condition cycle, the dedicated products remain the better option, especially for longer hair that needs stronger conditioning.

Hi,

You're asking how anyone can tell how fast a whole continent is sliding, and it's actually less mystical than it sounds. The main tool is GPS. Surveyors put fixed reference points on solid ground in different regions, and GPS receivers at those points keep logging their exact coordinates over weeks or years. The continents don't just stop moving, so the coordinates drift, and that drift is converted into a speed, usually in millimetres per year.

What matters is the network, not one station. A single receiver can be affected by local ground shifts, but when you have many stations, their average motion represents the plate or region as a whole. The positions are compared with a reference frame, and the difference between regions gives the relative speed of the plates.

There's more to it than land points. Satellite measurements of ocean surfaces and seafloor features add context, but for continents, ground-based GPS is the workhorse. It's a bit tedious, and the rates are tiny, but over time the numbers add up into a clear pattern.

Inbreeding does not lower IQ through a single obvious rule. The main mechanism is that related parents carry more of the same ancestry, so a child is more likely to inherit two copies of rare recessive genetic variants. Many genes influence brain development and learning, and some harmful variants only have an effect when present in two copies. When close relatives mate, the chance of a child being homozygous for such variants rises, which can reduce cognitive ability. This effect is statistical, not inevitable: some inbred children have normal IQ, and environment, nutrition, education and health still matter. Inbreeding depression is the term for the reduced fitness in offspring of related parents; lower average IQ is one visible part of that pattern. The reason this shows up as a group difference rather than a fixed individual score is that the variants are spread across many genes, each contributing a small amount.

Arm injuries often seem less painful than injuries to other areas, but that is not because arms are somehow spared. Pain is not just a signal from the wound; the brain weighs how important the area is, how much attention is given, and whether the injury threatens breathing, movement, or core function. Arm wound is often experienced as less catastrophic because the limb is not immediately life-critical in the same way the chest or head, and people can keep moving or using the arm. Tissue type matters too: skin, muscle, tendon and bone are all innervated, but the pattern of nerve endings and the brain’s interpretation differ by region. So a shot, stab, or blow to the arm may register as less urgent, not because the arm is numb, but because the nervous system and mind treat it as less threatening than an injury to a more central area.

Carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide do different things in your blood. Carbon dioxide is a normal byproduct of your cellular metabolism, and your lungs actively expel it. Carbon monoxide, on the other hand, has a terrible habit of binding to hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. It binds roughly two hundred times more strongly than oxygen does. This is a classic case of competitive inhibition. Once CO takes the binding site, oxygen simply cannot get in. It takes a long time to clear; the half-life of CO in the blood is roughly three to five hours on room air. You end up with carboxyhemoglobin, and your tissues starve for oxygen even if you are breathing pure air. That oxygen starvation is what makes it poisonous, leading to headaches, confusion, and eventually organ failure if exposure continues.

With carbon dioxide, you don't have that binding problem. Your body is built to handle it, constantly producing and clearing it. You only get into trouble with CO2 if the concentration in a room gets so high that it displaces the oxygen you need to breathe, or if it accumulates to the point of making your blood too acidic (respiratory acidosis), which drops the blood's pH. But under normal breathing conditions, CO2 just passes through. CO doesn't pass through; it stays put and blocks the oxygen. That's the whole issue.

It is a bit unfair to CO2, but it is mostly just a waste gas. The danger of CO is entirely about that hemoglobin binding. I wouldn't bother trying to explain it via combustion byproducts for this wiki; the hemoglobin mechanism is what a new colleague actually needs to understand why it's so lethal compared to CO2.

When an aircraft is in an emergency, the brace position is a short protective posture that reduces the chance of injury if the plane suffers a hard landing or sudden impact. The main idea is to keep your body as stable and compact as possible. You place your hands on your knees or grip your own arms or knees, keep your feet flat on the floor, and bring your head down and slightly forward. This is not the same as curling into a tight ball; it is a controlled, braced posture designed to manage forces during impact.

The protection comes from physics: during a crash or hard stop, unrestrained body parts keep moving and can strike interior surfaces or each other. By bracing, you limit the distance your head and neck can move, reduce the risk of neck injury, and spread impact forces across stronger body areas. You are also less likely to be thrown forward violently, and you can stay more predictable to cabin crew. Do not panic, and follow the crew's instruction. The position is therefore a simple but important safety habit: it does not prevent a crash, but it can reduce the injuries that follow a crash.

Most companies we know today survive because they could make, ship, and advertise to many people at once, something the industrial era made possible. Before that, businesses were usually local workshops, trading houses, or guild firms tied to particular customers, not mass consumers. A pre-industrial trading house might be famous among merchants, but its name would not appear on a shop shelf or in a national ad campaign. Standardized products, factory output, rail and steamship distribution, and trademark law are what let a name become household-level. So the absence is not because older firms did not exist; it is that the mechanisms for brand fame were thin before industry.

I’ve been through car finance a couple of times, and I’m not saying the dealer is always bad. But if I were buying a car today, I’d still take the bank’s offer. The dealer’s lower headline rate is often just that: a headline. The total you actually pay includes interest over the whole loan term plus any fees or add-on products the dealer tacks on. A lower annual percentage rate doesn’t mean a lower total cost if the loan is longer, if there’s a finance charge, or if you’re required to buy an extended warranty or a service plan. I’ve seen that pattern.

The bank’s loan may have a slightly higher rate, but it’s usually more transparent. You know the monthly payment, the total interest, and the exact amount you’ll pay over the term. The dealer’s finance office can present a lower rate and still come out more expensive because of the extras. That’s the part people miss. They look at the interest rate and assume that’s the whole picture. It isn’t.

For me, the deciding factor was the finance fee. The dealer quoted a lower APR, but then added a flat charge for processing the loan. The bank didn’t have that. When I did the math on the total repayment, the bank’s higher rate was offset by the absence of that fee. That’s the concrete difference. It wasn’t a small margin either. On a five-year loan, the difference added up fast.

You don’t have to guess. Ask both places for the total amount repaid over the full term, including all fees and add-ons. If the dealer’s total is higher, that’s the number to look at, not the advertised rate. I’d rather pay a bit more in interest each month and have no surprise charges at the end. That’s why I think financing through a bank is cheaper in practice, even when the dealer’s rate looks better on paper.

I keep going back to my aunt’s visit last spring. She had a prescription, yet the pharmacist in one state said no and another state said yes. That gap still annoys me.

I think the mess is mostly about who gets to decide. States can make their own rules, and that freedom is useful, but for something like marijuana it produces a patchwork. One county may sell it, another nearby town may still treat it like an old-school vice. The legality of marijuana in US states has changed so often that people plan trips or treatments around state lines, which is a bit absurd.

I’m not saying every state should agree. But I think a national baseline would help. At least people would know whether they can carry it, use it medically, or buy it legally.

I still find it strange that a body can make signals without a battery. Our cells create small voltages by moving ions, not storing them. Nerve cells use sodium-potassium pumps to keep sodium outside and potassium inside. When stimulated, sodium channels open; sodium floods in and the inside becomes less negative. That quick voltage shift is an action potential, moving along the nerve like a wave. The heart makes the same kind of electrical activity, which is why an ECG can read it. I keep coming back to this exact mechanism.

I have been thinking about how musicians sample older songs, and I want to push back on the idea that sampling is mostly theft. There is a difference between borrowing a recognizable riff and digging for a sound that fits a new track. I think the best sampling is less about the famous hook and more about treating an old record like a set of parts. Take a worn 1958 rhythm and bass figure from a forgotten R&B 45. You might chop it into small pieces, loop a four-bar pattern, pitch it down a half step, and bury it under a new drum beat. The listener may not identify the source, but the old song’s grain, the crackle, the slight swing, becomes part of the new piece. That is where the interest is.

For me the technical side is only part of the answer. A producer might import a recorded excerpt into a digital audio workstation, isolate a horn or vocal fragment, cut it into short slices, and rearrange those slices into a new groove. Or they might work with a turntable, scratching and looping a vinyl groove. Either way, the older song is not just pasted in. It is changed. I have heard tracks where a 1972 disco horn hit was sliced into six fragments, stretched, reversed, and placed between new hi-hats. The original song was still audible, but it had been turned into something else. That is the craft.

Licensing is the part people miss. If the sample is recognizable, the musician often has to clear rights with the songwriter and the owner of the recording. That can be slow and expensive, which is why some samples stay under the line of obvious recognition, or why a track gets pulled from a release. I think that pressure has shaped the form. The best samples sound like weather, not like quotations.

What I value most is the act of digging. A producer might spend hours in a record shop or on a listening archive, comparing needle drops until something catches. The older song becomes material for the present, not a monument. That is the position I want to take: sampling works when the past is handled as raw material and made to serve a new idea. I also wonder if this method is changing with streaming access to catalogs, but I still trust the old record as the starting point.

My headache is not a punishment. It happens because membranes, nerves, and blood vessels in my head get irritated or stretched. Last month I woke at four with a pressure behind my eyes. I was dehydrated from drinking coffee instead of water, and the pain flared as my blood vessels reacted. I have learned that when I sleep too little or sit too long at the computer, the head feels as if someone is tightening a band. The pain is my body’s warning, not illness. My position is simple: most headaches are my lifestyle talking, not my skull breaking. If I drink water, move, and give my eyes a rest, the tension eases. A sudden ache or fever deserves attention. But on ordinary days, the hurt is the head asking for care, and I have stopped blaming the air conditioning or the weather for what is really a small imbalance.

I can't say if the food was good because we never got to eat. We arrived at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday, and chose this place because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel and figured it would be easy. We entered our names into their completely useless digital waitlist, then were told to come back and pay at 8:23 p.m. We did, but then stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually mentioned we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15. It was a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait is going to stretch that far past payment, tell people upfront so our night isn't wasted. Absolute disaster. Zero stars if that were an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly there was no line at all. The meal for two came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than I had expected to pay there.

I was disappointed that steak wasn’t offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was that there were no proper crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian food station didn’t seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and an assortment of pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

Overall, I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

I’m keeping it, four stars. The space bar rattles; if you hit it with the edge of your thumb it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key repeats occasionally, so “example” becomes “eexample” and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I’m typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don’t ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I’d have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I still tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I've been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life, well the under-21 version of it, so I've sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught. Honestly? Mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

First the good: the circular stage is genuinely smart. You're basically looking down into it, so essentially any seat gets you a decent view. That's rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too: the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not a rip-off exactly; if you've seen Cirque, you've seen comparable feats, maybe with more clarity.

Clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don't know. There's a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it's trying to say. Also, way too much is happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing, where more must be better, so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you're staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal, $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn't pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn't blown away, and I don't think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you've never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don't expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago, we ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear by telephone. The shirts never arrived because the sales representative recorded the delivery address incorrectly: her handwritten 7 was read as a 1. The intended address was 5407, but the package was sent to 5401. The residents at 5401 took it to the local UPS store to return it, and then it disappeared and was never seen or heard from again. We did not really learn this until several weeks later. During the dispute, we ordered two more shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the original two shirts. The owner handled it; he acknowledged the shipment went to the wrong address but said no refund until the shirts were returned. He argued we were partly responsible because we had not been friendly enough to the residents at 5401, four doors away. We disputed the original charge with our credit-card company and eventually did receive a credit.
